tb21_profile.skill: Adversarial bypass of a sanitizer: read a filter that strips JavaScript from HTML, reason about where its removal is incomplete (parser quirks, comment/CDATA contexts, entity decoding, malformed tags, mutation-XSS), and craft an HTML file that survives the filter yet auto-executes alert() in a real browser.
tb21_profile.domain: Web security / XSS; browser HTML parsing and DOM semantics; HTML sanitization libraries (bleach, BeautifulSoup, markupsafe).
tb21_profile.task_form: reverse-engineer-a-filter-then-craft-an-evasion-payload (offensive): given a defensive script, produce an input that defeats it. Verified by a checker that both runs the filter and asserts the payload still fires.

verifier_notes: No grade I relied on was wrong. The CalibForge twin security_20260509_202829_001 is graded 'behavioral' (a test opens the sanitized output and asserts the alert still fires) - legitimately non-FREE and eligible for final_top10; I confirmed its instruction is essentially identical to the TB2.1 task, comment-parsing hint included. Terminal-Lego's task_07047 (implement an XSS-prevention library) is graded FREE, so it appears only in per_source with a note, not in final_top10.

SWE-Smith-Seeds-Clean.reason: The escape() function applies its character replacements in the wrong order, so entities are mis-escaped; a broken HTML escaper is precisely the flaw that lets script survive a filter.
Markup.striptags mishandles HTML comments; tag/comment stripping is exactly what filter.py does, and comment quirks are the classic bypass surface.
clean_attributes produces malformed HTML output; an HTML attribute cleaner going wrong is the same class of code as a JavaScript-stripping filter.
Bleach mishandles HTML entities inside anchor tags; bleach is the canonical HTML sanitizer and entity handling is where sanitizers are bypassed.
CSS-selector matching over a parsed DOM is broken; knowing exactly which nodes a selector-based cleaner catches or misses is what an evader exploits.
Conditional-comment tag rendering is wrong; conditional comments are a real IE-era XSS-smuggling vector, so the parsing edge case is on-topic.
Markdown-to-HTML ToC generation raises a TypeError; markup-to-HTML transformation is adjacent, but the bug is not about script removal.
Depth-limit and introspection validation logic is inverted, letting disallowed queries through; inverted validation is exactly how a filter fails open.
Delimiter handling at position 0 breaks in bleach's linkify; edge-of-string parsing bugs in a sanitizer, same family as boundary-based XSS bypasses.
soupsieve.escape() mis-escapes CSS identifiers; escaping-correctness bugs are the general class this XSS task turns on, in a CSS rather than HTML context.

escape() on exception descriptions; correct HTML-escaping of user-controlled text is the defense this task is designed to defeat.
URL-encoded path-segment decoding changed behaviour; encode/decode mismatch between layers is the mechanism behind many filter bypasses.
Duplicate text generation when RTL is involved in an HTML-to-PDF renderer; deep HTML/CSS rendering semantics, adjacent to browser parsing intuition.
CORS middleware emits an invalid header; a web security control that fails to enforce what it claims, same failure mode as an incomplete filter.
Fix a regex so it does not escape non-special characters; regex escaping correctness, the recurring weak point in string-based filters.
A '.' character is not escaped in a header value; an unescaped metacharacter is the kind of oversight an evader looks for.
A parser gives a false negative on SQL; parser blind spots are what injection and filter-bypass both exploit, though this is lineage analysis.
Verify BGP peer-group inheritance from device output; network-config parsing only, essentially no transfer to HTML/XSS.

notes: This is one of the strongest matches in the whole pool because CalibForge contains a near-literal twin (security_20260509_202829_001): same /app sanitizer, same 'make it still alert() after processing', same test_outputs.py, same comment-parsing hint. It is graded 'behavioral', not FREE, so it is a legitimate rank-1. CalibForge and Terminal-Lego together supply 6 of the final 10 and clearly beat the v1 pool - Lego's authored XSS tasks (analyse-XSS-beyond-encoding, why-regex-cannot-parse-HTML, the script-tag remover) are exactly the corpus note's promised HTML-sanitising strength, and CalibForge's whole family of 'bypass /app/filter.py' security tasks reproduces the task_form precisely. TMax's red-team evasion-payload tasks are the best of the v1 pool and hold two final slots. SWE-Smith is genuinely useful here on domain: bleach, markupsafe.striptags, python-readability and dominate are real HTML sanitizers/escapers, so their bugs teach the failure modes an evader exploits - one earns a final slot. SWE-Rebench is weaker (markdown/HTML renderers and escaping bugs, no adversary). Recursive-Task-Synthesis has NO graded verifier and no HTML-XSS task; its best offerings are payload/exploit-crafting chores (ExifTool CVE PoC, JWT alg-confusion, buffer-overflow exploits) that share the craft-an-adversarial-input skill but not the domain - all kept out of final in favour of graded equivalents. TerminalWorld's relevant items are binary-exploitation and one SQLi; decent skill transfer, wrong domain, and its shortlist was FREE-heavy. Downstream: this TB2.1 task is unusually well covered - if forced to pick one corpus, CalibForge alone gives four defensible finalists including the twin. task_07047 (Lego) is a strong-content XSS task held out of final only because its verifier is FREE.
